abstract: The reversible interconversion of rhodamines between nonfluorescent spirocyclic and fluorescent ring-open states underpins fluorogenic probes and spontaneously blinking dyes for super-resolution imaging. Existing strategies mainly tune the equilibrium between these states through electronic modification, whereas the role of conformational return in ring closure remains less explored. Here, we establish steric regulation of rhodamine spirolactams through amide N-substituents. Bulky substituents generate intramolecular repulsion with the xanthene scaffold, favoring ring opening. Crystallographic observations reveal substantial amide reorientation upon opening, suggesting increased separation between the nitrogen and meso-carbon reaction centers. We propose that substituent-dependent conformational accessibility modulates C-N bond reformation and the lifetime of the emissive state. The tert-butyl-substituted dye 1e exhibits an open-state residence time of 145 ms, despite its lower pKcycl. Calculations also indicate a lower ring-opening barrier for 1e than for less hindered 1a (1.12 vs 1.37 eV). Incorporating this design into HaloTag probes enables SIM, STED, and SMLM imaging. Importantly, N-halo-RBRB enables dual-modal SIM/SMLM imaging with a single fluorophore, integrating the rapid reconstruction of overall cellular architecture by SIM with single-molecule localization information from SMLM. This work identifies sterically modulated conformational accessibility as a design principle for engineering reversible rhodamine switches with tailored imaging capabilities.
